H 1, 10 mm; J, 2.5 mm Swan Islands and the Lesser Antilles, including Antigua, Barbuda, Guadeloupe, Dominica, Martinique, St Lucia, St Vincent, Aruba and Caraca. Maps 1 (p. 59), 56. It is probably indigenous to parts of coastal Venezuela and Guyana. It has also been recorded from Barbados, the reputed type locality, but no recent collections other than cultivated ones have been made. It has very recently been recorded from near Miami, continental United States of America. The species is common in coastal shrublands, forest or on the margins of mangroves on sand, saline clays or on limestone where it is often the dominant shrub. Although it favours dry exposed sites it will tolerate relatively high rainfall and in Puerto Rico it grows in areas that receive annual rainfalls up to 1800 mm. Like the majority of Myoporacee it favours open sunny situations.

Although a specimen labelled Bontia daphnoides is held at LINN (Savage Catalogue No. 812.1), an examination showed it not to be this species. The vegetative specimen superficially resembles Bontia in the shape of the leaf but the few irregular marginal notches are inconsistent with serrations occasionally found in Bontia and the venation is quite different. In addition, branches and leaves are pubescent, clothed in simple crisped hairs with the leaf buds being especially hairy. Linnaeus adopted the generic name Bontia, which had been first used by Plumier (1703) and supplemented it with information from Dillenius's treatment (1732). He also indicated in symbol form that he had seen material and it is possible that it was the above-mentioned specimen. He also placed Plukenet's 1694) "Olea, sylvestris barbadensis' in synonymy, and presumably his reference to Barbados as the origin was taken from Plukenet. Dillenius provided a detailed description and illustration of Bontia and the illustration depicted a leafy branch with buds and analytical drawings of calyx, gynoecium and fruit. No Dillenius specimen is held at OXF (see Clokie, account of Herbaria in OXF), but a copy of Dilleniuss 'Hortus Elthamensis' (1732) held at Friedrich Schiller University, Jena (JE), has been annotated throughout by Linnaeus (see H. Schmidt, Feddes Repert. Spec. Nov. Regni Veg. 70: 67--108), including the Bontia treatment. It was presumably used by Linnaeus to prepare his treatment for Genera Plantarum so it is selected as lectotype. It is presumed that Linnaeus misidentified the sterile specimen in the LINN herbarium. Gaertner (1791) recognised a second species B. minor, but from the description and illustrations of the fruit it appears that this was merely a smaller fruit ( immature form of B. daphnoides. This species is widely cultivated in the Caribbean as an ornamental or as a hedge or windbreak. It is quite salt tolerant.

Diocirea forms a link between Myoporum and Eremophila and shares features with both genera. The white to violet glabrous corolla (except for the inside of the lobes), the shallow tube with spreading lobes, the straight exserted stamens and the exposed gynoecium are features associated with Myoporum. However, Diocirea differs from Myoporum in having sessile, solitary flowers, with the upper 2 lobes of the corolla fused together for most of their length (except in D. ternata), a pubescent ovary, dry pubescent fruits, pubescent branches and very small, densely spiral, opposite or whorled leaves. The small, densely spiral to whorled leaves and sessile flowers are also found in a small group of entomophilous eremophilas found in sections Australophilae and A second feature which distinguishes Diocirea from Myoporum and Eremophila is the non-caducous corolla. The corolla attachment to the floral axis is small and situated underneath the ovary. Thus, although the abscession layer of cells is present at the corolla attachment, the ovary holds the corolla firmly in position and it is only as the fruit develops that the corolla may split and fall off. It is not uncommon to find old dried flowers of previous seasons scattered down the branches. Calamphoreus is the only genus in the family possessing a non-caducous corolla. Diocirea pollen differs from the other genera of Myoporaceae in the ornamentation of the exine, with all 4 species have a uniformly punctitegillate exine. In the other genera it is finely to coarsely reticulate. It is perhaps remarkable that none of the 4 species in this genus have previously been described, even though they occur in areas visited by such eminent late 19th and early 20th century botanists as L. Diels, E. Pritzel, S. Moore, C.A. Gardner and W. E. Blackall. The few collections of Diocirea located in herbaria have usually been filed under the name Eremophila elachantha Diels. Diocirea acutifolia is readily distinguished from the other species by its larger spreading linear-subulate leaves. Apart from the presence of resin at the branch tips this species, when in the vegetative state, could easily be mistaken for a member of the Epacridaceae. This species exudes resin, which eventually dries to form a white coating on the branches and leaves. In most cases the whitish resin only occurs as scattered patches but occasionally the whole plant can appear glaucous due to a very even covering on the leaves (Kuchel 1790). The quantity of resin exuded may be related to the moisture received, with larger quantities of resin being exuded in drier periods to reduce water loss.

Considerable leaf variation occurs in this species. In the commonest form the leaf is lanceolate with 1--3 pairs of prominent spreading or recurved teeth at the base and sometimes with a few obscure teeth near the apex. Domin's M. latisepalum was based on an oblanceolate leaf form lacking the basal teeth but with an obtuse apex with some teeth. The broadest leaf forms are found in this type. Flower colour also varies considerably, from white to lilac occasionally mauve (north of Chinchilla, Wilberforce). Allan (1961) in his description of the species in New Zealand refers to the flower colour as purplish, and living material studied at the Auckland Regional Authority Botanical Garden at Manurewa, presumably of New Zealand origin, had deep mauve flowers. Gardens, Manurewa, Auckland, New Zealand The New Zealand occurrence of this species is here treated as adventive. Allan (1961) first included E. debilis in the New Zealand flora, the species having been collected a few years earlier by R.O. Green on the coast between Kawhia and Raglan. Apparently Green found the species after following the directions of an elderly man over 80 years old who remembered seeing the plant in his boyhood. (P. de Lange, pers. comm.). Allan argued that because it was growing on a very remote part of the New Zealand coast it was unlikely that it was of garden origin. However, Mr P. de Lange (pers. comm.), who had made a study of the occurrence of this species in New Zealand and made extensive searches for it, is of the opinion, and I agree with him, that the species is an introduction. The reasons to support this are: 1. During the 1830s onwards there was a very active trade along this coast with Sydney and other Australian ports. 2. In this area there are also other odd Australian adventives, for example, Cassinia aculeata. 3. In 1977 J.K. Bartlett following R.O. Green's instructions tried to locate the original site and searched a gully between Papanuiti Point and Te Toto Gorge. He apparently did not locate the plant and mentioned evidence of recent fires. Given (1981) considered that fire may have wiped out the plant but I do not believe this as E. debilis is widespread in fire-prone areas in Australia and the well-developed tap-root with branches arising from its crown suggest that this species readily resprouts after fire. Peter de Lange visited the area and found numerous Australian plants in abundance, including Hakea salicifolia, H. gibbosa, Eucalyptus sp., Grevillea sp., Carex longibrachiata and others, on the cliffs abutting an old homestead 4. A population of 15 plants was found on a series of cliffs at Rengarenga Point in 1974. They were growing in pasture and scrub and according to Peter de Lange were very unhealthy and none survived beyond 1980. They appeared to have been planted and according to local knowledge (P. de Lange, pers. comm.) occurred in an area which equated with an old flour mill which ground wheat grown in the Oparau valley and then sold to Sydney. Artefacts in middens show that the inter-Tasman trade was well established in the 1830s. 5. The corolla colour found in plants cultivated in New Zealand is mauve (purplish according to Allan, 1961); however, in Australia the species normally has white flowers or white with a faint suggestion of lilac, and strongly-coloured forms are exceedingly rare in the wild. However, it is often these atypical forms that are selected for cultivation because of their more spectacular flowers. As Australian plants appeared to have be cultivated in areas along the Kawhia-Raglan coast which had an active trade with Australian ports it is likely that the more spectacularly-coloured flower forms of species would have been introduced by persons with an interest in Australian plants. Finally one cannot rule out the possibility that the introduction of E. debilis was accidental. It is quite conceivable that the species arrived in soil ballast discarded by a visiting ship to load grain for Sydney. Even if the ballast were discarded at sea the large fleshy fruits are quite capable of remaining afloat for more than 20 days, sufficient time for them to be washed ashore.

E. deserti occurs on a large variety of soil types including dark grey cracking clays, black soils, dark brown clays, red-brown sandy loams, yellow-brown silty loam, heavy red soils, sandy clay loams over granites, deep yellow sands and red-brown sands and on dunes. Throughout south-eastern Australia E. deserti is commonly found in Eucalyptus woodlands but in Queensland it is just as common in brigalow scrub. Occasionally it occurs in Callitris woodland In South and Western Australia it is common in Eucalyptus (mallee) woodlands, myall (Acacia papyrocarpa) and cypress pine (Callitris spp.) woodlands, Melaleuca shrublands, chenopodiaceous (Maireanal Atriplex) low shrublands and even on poorly drained soils in Halosarcial Nitraria low shrubland.

Leaf shape and size are extremely variable in E. deserti, ranging from long linear attenuated forms through to oblanceolate, obtuse-leaved ones. Very short, often obtuse-leaved forms appear to be more common in exposed coastal areas like along the Eucla escarpment and adjacent coastal plain (Hj. Eichler 21333, AD) or on offshore islands (Franklin Island, SA, D.C. Howlett 4B, AD). Leaf width also varies considerably and although typically 3--6 mm wide, extremely narrow forms with widths 0.8--1 mm are occasionally encountered (J.B. Cleland s.n. AD97609564). Fruit colour is also quite variable and although typically yellow to brownish yellow it can range to yellow tinged purple to dark brownish purple. A form which occurs in north-eastern Australia along the Great Dividing Range was first described by Mueller (1865) as which dilate distally, and leaves which are thinner and appear discolorous, although the thinner leaves are probably a result of habitat as this form appears to be associated with woodlands, occurring in more shaded and sheltered situations. Although many specimens of this form appear to be very distinct, many gradations to the more typical forms exist and population studies will be necessary to determine whether there is any sound basis for recognition at an infraspecific level. Forms of Eremophila deserti are known to be poisonous to stock, and 11 toxic furanoid sesquiterpenes have been isolated (see Everist, 1981), however, other forms of this species appear non-toxic with no ill effect on browsing animals (Everist 1947). No correlation between plant form and toxicity has yet been determined so all forms of E. deserti should be treated as toxic.

Eremophila eriocalyx is vegetatively a very uniform species, however, considerable variation occurs in corolla colour. Typically the corolla is cream and at bud stage either cream or bright lemon-yellow; however, in the western part of its range lilac to purple colour forms occur quite commonly (Bellairs 1839A, Holm 4). Occasional pink forms are also encountered (Wemm s.n., Chinnock 7255). One collection (Speck 1520) is atypical in having a glandular-pubescent corolla although a few branched hairs are also present. Eremophila physocalyx is closely related to E. eriocalyx (see Notes under that species). The illustration of E. eriocalyx done by Graff (Mueller, 1886) is consistent with the species except for features of the flower. The corolla does not posess the typical 'closed throat' of this species and it is shown to have exserted stamens. Furthermore, the dissected corolla does not appear to be woolly inside and is clearly glabrous outside. I suspect therefore that the flower used in preparing the illustration did not belong to E. eriocalyx but probably got mixed in with the material, which has been found H C GMD to be the case in other species illustrated by Graff

Eremophila forrestii is closely allied to E. glandulifera. See Notes under that species. Mueller based E. forrestii on a very fragmentary specimen with an immature flower in which the anthers had not yet become exserted so it is understandable why it was not considered by Bentham (E. leucophylla), Mueller (E. turtonii), Diels (E xanthotricha) and Fitzgerald (E. hastieana) when describing their new species. I have selected the Milne collection of E. leucophylla held at Kew, mounted on the sheet with a Helms collection, as lectotype for that name. The second sheet held at Kew (vegetative) is considered a syntype as is the Melbourne collection. E. turtonii was based on a form with obovate, cuneate leaves and obovate sepals but there is a complete gradation between this form and typical E. forrestii. E. xanthotricha was presumably recognised largely by the fact that the hairs on young growth were golden-yellow. However, this feature is of little significance as populations such as one examined south of Overlander Roadhouse (Chinnock 3794) consisted of a mixture of goldenand grey-haired forms with an approximate ratio of 1:1. Golden-haired forms appear to occur sporadically in many grey-tomentose species, including E. margarethae, E. latrobei and E punicea, but the condition is rare and it is usually confined to the young growth. In one species, E. citrina, it is the normal condition with grey-leaved forms being very rare. Barlow (1971) distinguished his E. sp. 2 from E. forrestii on the basis of its glabrous corolla, sessile flowers, valvate calyx-segments and larger leaves, gradually attenuated towards the base; however, this form is very close to the type of E. leucophylla and the corolla, like the fragmentary one present on the type specimen of E. forrestii, is not glabrous but obscurely glandular-pubescent. Eremophila glabra subsp. albicans is common throughout the South-West Botanical Province of Western Australia. The typical form of this subspecies occurs in coastal regions from Shark Bay to Bunbury and along the southern coast to near Cape Arid. It is characterised by having very minute stellate hairs less than 0.1 mm across on the vegetative parts. These hairs are only obvious towards the branch tips and especially in the dried state give the immature leaves a mealy appearance, whereas in older leaves the hairs are scattered or lost. In this form the flowers are orange-red or yellow and appear to vary in colour within some populations (R.J. Cranfield 359) A second inland form, which occurs throughout the Avon and Roe Botanical Districts, and has a few scattered records in the Austin Botanical District, may represent a second taxon. It differs in having narrower leaves and much larger, interlacing stellate hairs on the vegetative parts. More commonly the branches, leaves, pedicels and sepals are tomentose. The leaves may be entire or toothed and the flower colour variable from red to yellowish green. George Bentham's E. glabra var. viridiflora was based on a yellowish green flower form of this type. There also appears to be differences in fruit structure between the coastal and inland forms; however, although a large number of collections were examined relatively few were fruiting so I cannot be certain as to the consistency of fruit differences. Coastal forms have subglobular to globular fruits, which appear quite fleshy. In contrast the inland form has an ovoid, slightly fleshy fruit, which is constricted distally with a shallow furrow between the two carpels.

Eremophila maculata is one of the most widespread species in the genus. The structure of the flower is relatively uniform within the species with the exception of the colour and spotting. This can be extremely variable within and between populations of subsp. maculata. The shape of the leaf, however, is very variable and it is largely on this feature that the three subspecies are distinguished E. maculata subsp. maculata, widespread throughout the eastern and central States, is replaced in Western Australia, except in the Kimberley area and along the Nullarbor, by subsp. brevifolia, a smaller often divaricate shrub with distinctly petiolate, elliptic, obovate or suborbicular leaves. In this Eremophila maculata subsp. subspecies the flower is less variable in colour and commonly carmine and without spotting. In subsp. maculata flower colour varies through carmine, brick-red, brownish red to pure yellow and occasionally bluish purple. The flowers are usually prominently spotted within the tube or on the lobes, although in some yellow forms the spotting is absent. Spotting can vary greatly within a population. Within subsp. maculata there is considerable variation in the degree of tomentum on the branches and in the shape of the leaf. Widespread and abundant throughout central and eastern Queensland and north-central New South Wales where it is often a major woody weed. It grows on duplex soils, clays, earths and sands and forms a major component of most woodlands, and invades pastureland. A detailed Eremophila mitchellii account of the ecology and control of this species is provided by Beeston and Webb (1977). It is common in a variety of vegetation communities including brigalow (Acacia harpophylla), wilga (Geijera parvifolia), belah (Casuarina cristata), gidgee (Acacia cambagei), mulga (Acacia aneura), white cypress pine (Callitris glaucophylla), leopard wood (Flindersia maculosa) and tumble box (Eucalyptus populnea).

Eremophila mitchellii is very close to E. sturtii and it is often difficult to distinguish between these two species. Smith (1975) separated the two on the basis of flower colour, corolla pubescence and leaf shape and although these are very useful characters none of them are absolute. Two features found to be consistently different were the number of flowers in the axil, and the bark. The bark of E. mitchellii is only shallowly fissured and flakes into small pieces with the basal part of each piece curling outwards. In E. sturtii, if a trunk is formed, the bark is thick, firm and deeply fissured. Normally there is a solitary flower in the axil of E. sturtii although sometimes an odd branch will produce paired flowers while.in E. mitchellii there are two or three flowers in each axil. Sometimes in E. mitchelli only one flower develops although the aborted second (and third) bud is always visible. In most cases flower colour and pubescence will distinguish between the two species. The outside of the floral tube of E. mitchelli is very sparsely obscurely glandular-puberulent to almost glabrous and the corolla white, although, very rarely, pink to mauve forms do occur (Muffet MS/329, CBG). In contrast, the corolla tube of E. sturtii is densely pubescent, mauve to pinkish mauve in colour or, more rarely, almost white. Considerably more variation was found in the indumentum of the ovary and fruit of E. mitchellii than reported by Smith (1975). Although the fruit is commonly densely villous with numerous shorter glandular hairs, the longer villous hairs may become very scattered or absent with the fruit being only glandular-pubescent. In populations adjacent to the coast in the Townsville region the ovary is completely glabrous (Chinnock 5834, AD; Lazarides & Storey 35, CANB). The fruit type in E. sturtii is uniform over its range. The timber of E. mitchelli is fine grained and often called rosewood. It is also scented and has been exported to China in the past as an incense substitute. It is a light wood but very tough and resistant to white ants (Anderson, 1968). Rabbits freely eat the bark when other food sources are scarce, and twigs and bark have been used with strychnine for poison bait (Anderson, 1968).

Eremophila oppositifolia possesses one of the least specialised ornithophilous flower types. The corolla lobes are broad, obtuse and similar in size although the upper pair are fused for most of their length. The stamens are exerted to the tip of the upper pair of lobes or just beyond them. These features, together with the large sepals, suggest that E. oppositifola is closely allied to E. platycalyx subsp. pardalota. It differs from E. platycalyx in the size and shape of the leaves, the absence of spotting on the corolla, and the size and shape of the fruit. Although the structure of the flower and fruit is uniform over the whole range of the species, considerable variation does occur in the vegetative parts and it is upon differences in leaf shape and arrangement that the three subspecies are recognised. Subsp. angustifolia is the common taxon throughout Western Australia. Typically it forms a tall shrub or small tree with a rounded crown. The leaves are typically terete, oppositely arranged and usually short, straight and rigid, never becoming Alexuose as in the type subspecies. In the extreme north-western part of its range, leaves are flattened as they are in subsp. rubra. The flower, as in the type subspecies, is typically cream tinged pink above, although one striking variant was found in a population east of Dallwallinu. In this population many individuals possessed flowers with dark maroon sepals and corollas while others had the normal colour form with cream sepals. Many intermediate colour shades were also present. Over most of its range the type subspecies forms a straggly shrub rarely approaching tree proportions. The leaves are opposite, flexible and flexuose. The leaves are typically flattened on the upper side and slightly folded so that they are distinctly channelled above. In the north-western and south-eastern parts of the range of this subspecies, intergrades with subsp. angustifolia (north-west) and subsp. rubra (south-east) occur. There is no question that the different collections of E. oppositifola made near Emu, Great Victoria Desert, belong to subsp. angustifolia and some populations in the Gawler Ranges are perhaps best included under this subspecies. However, in the Gawler Ranges and Eyre Peninsula, subterete forms approach subsp. angustifolia but in these cases some leaves are usually broader and flatter and all are distinctly flattened on the upper side. Along the South Australian border and adjacent regions in Victoria and New South Wales from Broken Hill southwards forms of subsp. oppositifolia approach subsp. rubra.

Eremophila platycalyx is an extremely polymorphic species, especially with respect to leaf shape and the shape and spotting of the corolla. Broad-leaved forms of the species are largely concentrated in the eastern part of the species range, and it is considered that Kraenzlin (1929) based his species E .123b. subsp. pardalota dielsiana (type destroyed) on this form. Furthermore, Kraenzlin's E. platycalyx var. Lancifolia described on the same paper was also based on this broad-leaved form but in this case he did not appear to have seen any dried material, merely describing the variety upon the top right-hand figure depicted in Graff's illustration of E. platycalyx in Mueller's 'Myoporinous Plants of Australia' (1866). Although extreme narrow- and broad-leaved forms of E. platycalyx appear very distinct, complete intergrading between these forms occurs. The flowers within a population of subsp. platycalyx may be uniform or vary markedly from plant to plant although for an individual the corolla form is constant. The cream corolla may be prominently spotted blackish purple outside with the anthers commonly exserted to the throat or just beyond the lobes of the upper lip, or it may be unspotted, in which case the anthers are enclosed within the throat. In subsp. pardalota the corolla is uniformly narrow tubular, prominently spotted outside and D the stamens exserted to the lobes of the upper lip. This is the only species of Eremophila showing floral adaptations to both ornithophily and entomophily within different populations with many intermediate stages. Eremophila santalina usually forms a small tree with weak drooping branches, although at the shrub stage the branches are erect and it can be easily mistaken for either E. deserti or E. fallax; however, the thinner leaves which are attenuated to both base and apex and the larger, smooth, shiny brown fruit readily distinguish this species. In his protologue account of Pholidiopsis santalina, Mueller provided descriptions of flowers and fruit including measurements. Mueller collected this species at Cudnaka but of the three herbarium sheets attributed to Mueller held at MEL, there is only one that has a direct reference to this locality. This sheet (MEL 77714) has a small portion of vegetative branch and two associated labels. One white label in Mueller's hand has 'Pholidiopsis santalina Ferd. Mueller, Myoporinae' at the top, followed by a description of the plant which continues on to the other side of the label. This description gives details of flowers and at the bottom there is reference to Cudnaka and a date of Oct. 51, followed by Eremophila santalina and Dr M, indicating that he was the collector. The other two collections that appear to be part of this gathering are consistent with the Cudnaka specimen and have labels in Mueller's hand. One sheet (MEL 83702) has two associated labels, one pink with Pholidiopsis santalina written in Mueller's hand and the other blue, which originally formed part of one of Mueller's small folded packets, commonly made to enclose fragments or dissected flowers, and has Eremophila santalina written on it. Both these labels have been initialled by Bentham. This specimen has buds and one fruit. The other sheet, MEL 83701, has two large portions of branch possessing flowers with corollas, and a cellophane bag with fragments including one fruit. There is a label in Mueller's hand with 'n.g. Pholidiopsis santalina Ferd Mueller, N. Holl. Austr. interior, Ferd Mueller'. According to Grandison (1990), Mueller visited the Flinders Ranges only once and as he would have been limited in what he could collect and carry, it is reasonable to assume that he made one gathering of Pholidiopsis santalina and that the three specimens at MEL, attributed to Mueller, are part of the one collection. Certainly Mueller's protologue description could not have been based upon the 'Cudnaka' specimen, as it is vegetative. Mueller had a habit of providing different wording on labels of what appear to be duplicates and according to Dr J. Ross (pers. comm.), it is not unusual to find no label that bears the precise wording provided by Mueller in his protologue. I have therefore lectotypified upon the most complete specimen possessing flowers and fruits (MEL 83701) and the other two sheets are considered syntypes.

It also favours more saline situations than E. battii. One feature of this species is the ability to defoliate during prolonged dry periods and when in this condition confirmation can usually be made by searching under the shrub and finding the fruits. These get caught up in the tangle of branches, which occur at ground level. In very moist situations and in cultivation branches rarely become spinescent and are usually not rigid. This species, like E. elderi and its relatives, has solid-coloured bands instead of spotting on the lateral walls of the tube, which may suggest a link with this group.

Eremophila spuria superficially resembles a number of species including E. granitica, E. hughesii and narrow-leaved forms of E. clarkei; however, it is closely related to E. hughesii and E. setacea. These three species possess a characteristic swollen sepal apex, most pronounced in E. spuria, which distinguishes them from forms of E. clarkii and E. granitica. E. spuria is distinguished from E. setacea by the prominently glandular-pubescent sepals, the more resinous leaves and branches and the usually more slender leaves' and from E. hughesii by the nonweeping habit and obtuse corolla lobes. Eremophila veronica is a relatively uniform species over its range although one collection from west of Norseman differs in having pubescence on the abaxial leaf surface and non-tuberculate branches. The Diels type of Eremophila elachantha was destroyed in Berlin and I have been unable to locate duplicates elsewhere. The protologue does not adequately define the species and could be applied to a number of species. An illustration accompanying the description, consisting of a flowering branch and an enlarged flower, suggest that it is possibly a form of E. veronica, although the corolla appears too elongated for that species. Previously Myoporum subserratum Nees has been included in the synonymy of M. tetrandrum, and although I include it here in the synonymy of M. caprarioides, the type specimen has features to suggest that it is probably a hybrid between this species and M. insulare R. The unique twiggy habit and leaf form of M. cordifolium makes it stand apart from the other species in the genus. Flower and fruit structure also support this link. and developing fruits Leaf development of a seedling (based on a number of seedlings) is as follows. The first two leaves (following cotyledons) are opposite, oblanceolate, obtuse, entire, 22 × 3 mm. Leaves 3 and 4 are subopposite, oblanceolate, acute and distinctly toothed in the distal half. They are slightly shorter than leaves 1 and 2 but broader, 20 x 5.5 mm. The fifth leaf is alternately arranged, oblanceolate, acute and irregularly coarsely toothed, with incurved teeth and the surface faintly tuberculate. It is half the length of the previous leaf, 10 × 3 mm. Leaf 6 is ovate-triangular, 6.5 × 3.5 mm. Leaves 7 to 9 gradually decrease in size and are more erect and incurving towards the branch, and by leaf 10 the adult form is attained. Variation in the number of leaves involved in the transition from juvenile to adult leaf is dependent on conditions, with vigorous, rapidly growing seedlings usually producing more juvenile leaves (AD 98951231). It was also noted that lateral shoots which developed in the leaf axils of the first leaf pair formed adult leaves immediately although the first two leaves were slightly larger and comparable with leaves 8 and 9 on the main axis. Germination of seed from freshly collected fruits is slow. Fruits sown in a pot (March 31, 1988) were buried just below the soil surface and regularly watered, but only one seedling had appeared by September of that year. In late September, the pot was removed from the glasshouse and placed outside in full sun. A rapid germination occurred at the beginning of May 1989, following relatively mild temperatures and good soaking rains, and 17 seedlings had appeared by May 4, 29 by May 17 and 61 by May 19. It would appear that this species, like many species of Eremophila, requires a period of weathering ( to high summer temperatures) before germination will occur. In the case of the population studied near Gairdner River (Chinnock 4942) it would appear that the species responds rapidly, especially in disturbed sites, to good autumnwinter rainfall, resulting in a rapid germination and seedling development with flowering occurring within 12--15 months. Plants at this population were numerous and appeared to be all of a similar age, suggesting a mass germination at the site. The species is thought to be short-lived.

Myoporum montanum is an extremely variable, ubiquitous species within which three forms can be distinguished but because of inadequacies of dried herbarium material and the intergrades which link these forms I have refrained from recognising infraspecific taxa in this treatment. Detailed population studies, especially along the coastal areas of Queensland and northern New South Wales, will be necessary to determine consistency of morphological characters before a meaningful subdivision can be developed. The three forms that are recognised are discussed below: a) TYPE form - Robert Brown based the species on a narrow-leaved form found in the Blue Mountains. It is particularly common in the West Wyalong-Temora-Coolamon area. This form typically has narrow linear leaves 3--5 mm broad and small white unspotted or faintly spotted flowers, <8 mm in diameter. The flowers are bisexual or functionally dioecious. b) DESERT form - Throughout the arid areas of Western Australia, southern Northern Territory, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and along the Murray River in north-western Victoria occurs a form which forms a large shrub or small tree. It has thick linear-elliptic leaves in which the venation is obscured except for the basal part of the midrib. The flowers are bisexual, usually 10--15 mm in diameter, white and prominently spotted red-purple to purple. c) TROPICAL form - Extending along coastal and adjacent regions from Broome, across the north and down the eastern coast to northern New South Wales as well as in New Guinea and Timor is a form first recognised by Bentham (1870) as M. acuminatum var. parviflorum. This form has very small white unspotted flowers rarely reaching 8 mm in diameter. Unlike the Desert form this has thin leaves with obvious venation and discolorous surfaces although I am not certain whether the two surfaces are always discolorous. It would appear that in this form the flowers can be bisexual or functionally male or female. Populations studied near Ipswich were found at one site to consist of functionally female plants (R.J. Chinnock 8285) and at another a few kilometres away only bisexual plants (R.J. Chinnock 8284). As in Eremophila deserti, the male flowers are slightly larger with prominent anthers and a long style with an undeveloped stigmatic apex. Female flowers have small, undeveloped anthers and a short style with a large papillose stigmatic apex. It has also been noted in populations of M. insulare around Adelaide that frequently plants within populations may be functionally bisexual or female and it is suspected, from the examination of herbarium collections, that other species may vary from the normal bisexual condition too. Bloembergen (1951) referred to 4- and 6-lobed corollas in Malesian material, however, I have only noted 5-lobed ones in km Map 33 Distribution of Myoporum montanum Australian populations although variations from 5 have been noted in other Australian species.

Myoporum stellatum is restricted to the coral plain on the south-west corner of O'ahu between Pearl Harbour and Barbers Point although now extinct at many sites. There is one old record for Kaua'i Island, which is considered doubtful. It occurs on coralline sandy loams and at Kalaeoloa (Barbers) Point was associated with Hibiscus tiliaceus, Ipomea pes-caprae, Rhagodia semibaccata, Capparis, Lycium and Sporobolus.

Although M. stellatum has been treated as a variety of M. sandwicense, I am quite satisfied that it should be recognised at species level. It is more closely related to M degeneri, which has similar-structured glandular hairs although they are all simple. The simple or stellate to substellate indumentum found on the vegetative and floral parts of these two species is unique within the family, both in the colour and structure of the hairs. Although there are numerous branched hair types in Eremophila none appear analogous to those found in M. stellatum and M. degeneri. Although well-defined hairs are developed in other species of Myoporum, for example, M. sandwicense, M. crassifolium (sometimes), M. betcheanum, M. velutinum, these hairs are simple eglandular ones. Short glandular hairs may occasionally occur on sepal margins in these and other species and in M. betcheanum they are intermixed with longer eglandular hairs on vegetative parts, but these glandular hairs are consistent with types found in Eremophila. The development of the branched hairs in M. stellatum can be followed during seedling development (see Chinnock, AD 99508016). The cotyledons and hypocotyl of the seedling are prominently glandular-pubescent with all hairs simple as in M. degeneri. The first two leaves, which are oppositely arranged, have some simple glandular hairs but these are much shorter than those of the cotyledons and are largely confined to the margins in the distal part of the leaves. By the second leaf pair the glandular hairs have contracted to sessile glands and there is no evidence of any branched hairs. Successive leaves are alternately arranged with simple glandular hairs beginning to develop again on the stem and leaves, but by leaf 6, only branched hairs develop. Between leaf 8 and leaf 12, the branched hairs are few and scattered but most frequent along the midrib. The density and cover of branched glandular hairs gradually increases with successive leaves. Webster (1951) noted that the fifth stamen was often lost in this species; however, I noted in the Barbers Point population some corollas with 4 or 6 lobes, and with 1 or a number of non-functional stamens. Variations, particularly in the number of corolla lobes and stamen number, occur in other species apart from the Hawaiian ones-M. viscosum, for example, may have up to 8 lobes and 7 stamens and M. brevipes 4 lobes. In M. insulare quite often all 4 stamens are non-functional in a given flower, depending on when the flowers are produced. More irregularities appear to occur at the beginning or end of a flowering season.

Pentacoelium bontioides is restricted to coastal areas in southern Japan, including the Ryukyu Archipelago, and South China, including Taiwan and Hong Kong. It grows in mangrove situations along beaches at high tide line or along inlets and in coves free of strong wave or surf action. In Japan it is often associated with the sea-grass Zoysia sinica var. nipponica.
